children.text: Nineteen components, shared stage gates, one January 2028 deadline, three statutory predecessors and the closeout obligations of a withdrawn federal agreement. Chapter 15 concludes that this is not a problem component managers can solve by working harder or coordinating better among themselves. It needs a single designated authority with the mandate and the access to manage the transformation as a whole: a Portfolio Manager.

This lesson defines that role as the book does: what the Portfolio Manager does, the authority the role must carry to be useful, the credential that fits it, and where the role should sit. It also explains why contracted support, however expert, cannot fill it.

The central message is that the role is defined by its authority more than its tasks. Many people can maintain a register or chair a meeting. Only a role with the power to sequence work can change what the portfolio delivers.
Why One Integrator

Component managers optimize their components. That is their job, and they should do it well. But a portfolio's most important decisions are the ones no component manager can make: which component gets scarce staff this quarter, which one should wait for an upstream dependency, which one should be stopped because its benefits are no longer achievable. Left to negotiation among peers, those decisions default to whoever has the nearest deadline or the loudest sponsor.

Chapter 15's Implications section puts the point sharply for state leaders. Vermont does not lack oversight: it has the Health Care Advisory Committee (HCAC), monthly legislative reporting and federal review. What it lacks is an integrator, one role accountable for the portfolio as a whole, with authority to resolve resource conflicts between components that today are managed by different units against different deadlines.

The idea is not new to Vermont. Oliver Wyman's Act 167 report recommended a dedicated project-management function to manage the state's transformation portfolio, the November 2025 transformation report repeated the finding, and the AHS restructuring analysis in Chapter 16 identifies establishing a portfolio office as a critical organizational project. Chapter 15's contribution is a precise definition of the role.
The single most consequential decision is not whether to hire a Portfolio Manager but whether that role is given authority over sequencing. (Transforming Healthcare, Chapter 15)
What the Portfolio Manager Does

The book lists the role's responsibilities in summary. The Portfolio Manager chairs the monthly portfolio review board and maintains the portfolio register and the risk register. The role authorizes components being added to or removed from the portfolio, keeps every component aligned to Act 167's five statutory goals, and resolves resource conflicts between components.

The role also faces outward. It owns the Vermont Scorecard reporting to the HCAC and the AHS Secretary, manages portfolio-level relationships with the HCAC, the Green Mountain Care Board, hospital chief executives, the Legislature and CMS, and tracks benefits realization, recommending that a component be terminated when its benefits are no longer achievable.

Read the list for what is missing as much as what is present. The Portfolio Manager does not run components, write rules, design payment models or manage hospitals. Every duty concerns the portfolio as a whole: its composition, its alignment, its resources, its risks, its benefits and its story to the people who oversee it.

children.text: Authority Is the Job

A Portfolio Manager without authority becomes a reporting function: it documents the portfolio's problems without being able to fix them. The book specifies the authority the role needs. It reports directly to the AHS Secretary, with a co-reporting relationship to the Green Mountain Care Board. It holds budget authority over the transformation PMO. And it can require reporting from all nineteen component leads.

The most important power is over sequencing. The book is direct: a portfolio office that reports status without the power to hold a component back until its upstream gate opens will document the failure cascade rather than prevent it. Holding a component back is uncomfortable, because the component's sponsors will see it as a delay. It is also the single decision that most distinguishes a managed portfolio from a list of projects.

Authority also has limits, and the book draws them clearly when answering the objection that hospitals will not accept being managed by AHS. The Portfolio Manager does not manage the hospitals. It manages AHS's contribution to the portfolio. Hospital plans are produced by hospitals, approved by AHS and monitored through the Green Mountain Care Board. The role is an orchestrator, not a controller.

children.text: The Credential: PMI Portfolio Management Professional

The book names PMI's Portfolio Management Professional (PfMP) credential as the appropriate one for the role, together with substantial program or portfolio experience and experience in health systems or large-scale government programs. The PfMP is PMI's credential for practitioners who manage portfolios aligned to organizational strategy.

PMI's current eligibility rules offer three paths, all requiring 96 months (eight years) of professional business experience within the past fifteen years. With a secondary diploma, a candidate also needs 84 months of portfolio-management experience. With a bachelor's degree or higher, the requirement is 48 months. With a degree from a program accredited by PMI's Global Accreditation Center, it is 36 months. Requirements change, so check PMI's current exam content outline before relying on these figures.

A credential is evidence of method, not a substitute for judgment. For a state transformation, the book pairs it with health-system or government program experience, because the hardest parts of the job are political and institutional: persuading agencies to share resources, telling a sponsor that their component must wait, and explaining the portfolio's logic to a legislature.

children.text: Where the Role Sits, and What Contractors Cannot Do

For Vermont, the book places the role at the level of the AHS Secretary, or as a dedicated chief portfolio officer. For a hospital or health system, the equivalent sits close to the chief executive or chief strategy officer, above the individual program leads. In either case the test is the same: can the role move resources and change the order of work across organizational boundaries? If not, it is placed too low.

The fifth objection the book answers is that AHS already has expert help. Its March 2026 Act 68 report lists contracted transformation support from Manatt, Phelps & Phillips, a new hospital technical-assistance vendor, and analytics support under negotiation. The book's reply is that a contractor delivers a defined scope. It cannot hold a state component back until its upstream gate opens, reassign agency staff between components, or answer to the Legislature for the portfolio as a whole.

Contracted support adds capacity, not authority. Worse, every new contract is one more component, with its own deliverables and deadline, that someone has to sequence. The more expert help a transformation buys, the more it needs a portfolio manager to integrate it.

Timing matters as much as placement. The book's roadmap puts a Portfolio Manager in the seat by January 2027, nine months before FY2028 hospital budgets take effect in October 2027, so the role is running before the Technology gate it is meant to protect. A portfolio manager hired after the gating decisions have been made can only report on their consequences.

body.message: A coordinator who schedules meetings and compiles reports is useful, but it is not the role Chapter 15 describes. If the person cannot resolve a resource conflict or hold a component back, the portfolio still has no integrator.
body.title: Do not appoint a coordinator and call it a portfolio manager

points: A transformation of Vermont's scale needs a single integrator, because the portfolio's key decisions cannot be made by component managers negotiating among themselves.
Vermont has oversight bodies but no integrator: no role accountable for the whole with authority over resource conflicts between components.

The Portfolio Manager chairs the review board, maintains the portfolio and risk registers, keeps components aligned to Act 167's goals, resolves resource conflicts, owns Scorecard reporting and tracks benefits.
The role needs authority: a direct report to the AHS Secretary, a GMCB co-reporting line, budget authority over the PMO and power to require reporting from every component lead.
The decisive power is over sequencing: without it, a portfolio office documents the failure cascade instead of preventing it.
PMI's PfMP requires 96 months of business experience plus 84, 48 or 36 months of portfolio experience depending on education.
Contractors add capacity, not authority, and each new contract is another component someone has to sequence.

body.explanation: The book is explicit that a portfolio office reporting status without power over sequencing will document the failure cascade rather than prevent it. Hospital plans are approved by AHS and monitored through the GMCB, not run by the Portfolio Manager, and contractors add capacity rather than authority.
